newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan urges India to be "realistic" in talks.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan urges India to be "realistic" in talks.

text.p: Pakistan's President Farooq Leghari urged Indian leaders on Wednesday to take a realistic stance on Kashmir to allow revived dialogue to flourish.
"We would expect the Indian leadership to demonstrate more realism during the resumption of talks," Leghari said in an address to a joint sitting of both houses of parliament.
He was referring to talks between the top diplomats of the Indian and Pakistani foreign ministries which are due to resume in New Delhi on Friday after a three-year break.

"(Then) it would be possible for the two big countries of South Asia to have good relations free of bitterness and rift so that both countries can spend part of their incomes on improving the condition of their people," Leghari said.

The last round of foreign secretary-level talks collapsed in January 1994 over the dispute on Kashmir -- a mostly Moslem region which has been divided between the two countries since shortly after their birth as independent states in 1947.

Leghari said Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub would meet his Indian counterpart Inder Kumar Gujral. Their talks are expected to take place on the sidelines of, or after, a Non-Aligned Movement meeting in New Delhi on April 7 and 8.
"As a result of the stages of these talks, it is possible that even higher-level talks take place," Leghari said.
He appeared to be referring to a possible meeting between the two prime ministers in May in the Maldives, venue of a summit of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation.

"But the condition is that India should adopt a realistic approach and should agree to implement the promise it had made to a world body and world nations to give Kashmiris their fundamental right of self-determination," Leghari added.

Pakistan has long insisted that the Kashmir conflict can be solved by implementing decades-old U.N. resolutions calling for a plebiscite to allow Kashmiris to choose whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
India rejects the idea, saying Kashmir is an integral part of its territory.
Leghari said Pakistan had in the past agreed to third-party mediation of its quarrel with India and some friendly countries had agreed to play that role.
"But unfortunately the Indian attitude was not encouraging, because of which there has been no worthwhile progress so far in resolving the fundamental disputes," he said.
Leghari said Pakistan could not afford to drop its guard at a time when India had "substantially" boosted defence spending.

"We do not want to take part in an arms race but we cannot overlook our defence requirements. We need to maintain a reliable defence capability under all circumstances so that no one can cast an evil eye on us," the president said.
Pakistan and India have fought three wars since 1947, two of them over Kashmir. Both countries deny possessing nuclear bombs, but Western officials say both could assemble them swiftly.
